title: Theoretical Insights into Fine-Tuning Attention Mechanism: Generalization and Optimization

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to explain the "Unequal Importance of Attention Matrices" phenomenon and justify why fine-tuning only \( W_q \) and \( W_v \) is preferable to fine-tuning all three matrices (\( W_q, W_k, W_v \)). No prior paper explicitly establishes or explains this specific empirical relationship between the gradients of \( W_q, W_k, W_v \) and their importance in fine-tuning. While some papers discuss fine-tuning strategies (e.g., [5], [7], [17], [21]), none address this particular phenomenon or provide a theoretical justification for the unequal importance of attention matrices. Thus, the purpose is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses an information-theoretic generalization analysis to establish bounds (Theorem 1) for fine-tuning pre-trained attention models, showing that fine-tuning \( W_q \) and \( W_v \) reduces parameters while improving generalization bounds. Papers such as [1], [3], [8], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], and [18] discuss information-theoretic generalization bounds, but none specifically analyze fine-tuning attention matrices or derive bounds motivated by the gradient behavior of \( W_q, W_k, W_v \). The mechanism is **not covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation includes both theoretical (Theorem 1 generalization bound) and empirical validation, showing that fine-tuning \( W_q \) and \( W_v \) yields better performance than fine-tuning \( W_k \) or all three matrices, while reducing tunable parameters. Papers such as [5], [7], [17], and [21] evaluate parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, but none use the same evaluation design (theoretical generalization bound combined with empirical validation of attention matrix importance). Thus, the evaluation design is **not covered**.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) and attention mechanism theory. Papers such as [5], [7], [17], and [21] address parameter-efficient fine-tuning in LLMs, and papers such as [6], [16], and [23] study attention mechanisms. Therefore, the domain is **covered**.

### Purpose
The contribution aims to explain the phenomenon that assigning a higher learning rate to \( W_v \) in attention matrices leads to better convergence. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish this specific empirical relationship between learning rates of \( W_v \) and convergence dynamics in attention mechanisms. While some papers discuss learning rate adaptation (e.g., [9], [14], [18]), they do not address this particular phenomenon or justify the relationship between \( W_v \) and convergence.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves analyzing the learning dynamics of attention mechanisms, specifically showing inefficient learning in \( W_v \) (Case 1) and deriving scaling arguments for large-width networks (Theorem 2) to justify assigning a higher learning rate to \( W_v \). Papers such as [1], [8], [15], and [23] analyze learning dynamics in neural networks, including attention mechanisms and infinite-width scaling, but none derive scaling arguments or analyze \( W_v \) learning inefficiency in the same way. The specific mechanism of scaling arguments for \( W_v \) learning rate adjustment appears absent in prior work.

### Evaluation
The evaluation facet involves Theorem 2, which theoretically validates efficient feature learning under large-width scaling when \( W_v \) has a higher learning rate relative to \( W_q \) and \( W_k \). Papers such as [5], [8], [15], and [23] use theoretical scaling arguments and asymptotic analysis for wide networks, but none employ the same evaluation design or theoretical framework to validate learning rate adjustments for \( W_v \). The evaluation design appears novel.

### Domain
The domain is optimization and learning-rate tuning for attention fine-tuning. Papers such as [9], [14], [18], and [25] address learning-rate tuning and optimization in deep networks, including layer-wise or adaptive learning rates. While these papers do not specifically target attention mechanisms, the general application area of optimization and learning-rate tuning is covered.
